Stage 01 · View

Spot the difference

Read the five sentences. Do not open the rules yet. What changes when the speaker means “in general”, “one”, “specific”, “unique” or a profession?

8 min

Five clues

A. I think arguments are normal.
B. The arguments I have with my parents are about my bedroom.
C. I’m in an unusual situation.
D. He’s the headmaster at my school.
E. My mum’s a doctor.
A = Ø for general plural nouns · B = the for a specific group · C = an for one singular thing mentioned for the first time · D = the for something unique in that context · E = a for a profession.
1b · Language detective: Are rules 1–5 similar in your language? Choose one rule that feels different and explain why.
Stage 01
Notice the pattern: tiny article words change the whole message.
Stage 02 · View → Practice

Build the rule map

Use the clues from the warm-up, then compare with the clean rule map below.

12 min
a/an

One / first mention

Use a/an with a singular countable noun when it appears for the first time or means “one of many”.

a probleman idea
a/an

Profession

Use a/an to say what somebody does.

a teacheran engineer
the

Specific / known

Use the when both people know which person or thing we mean, or it was mentioned before.

the problemthe photos
Ø

In general

Use no article with plural countable or uncountable nouns when speaking generally.

musicteenagers

Unique = the

There is only one in the situation or world.

the headmaster · the sun · the world

Sound, not spelling

an before a vowel sound; a before a consonant sound.

an hour · a university

Useful chunks

Some phrases naturally use the or Ø.

the same · the government · have dinner

1Complete rules 1–5 with a/an, the or no article.
1. We use when we talk about things in general.
2. We use to talk about a specific person or thing, or a person or thing mentioned before.
3. We use to talk about a singular, countable person or thing for the first time, or to say it is one of a number of people or things.
4. We use to talk about someone or something that is unique.
5. We use to say what somebody’s profession is.
Stage 03 · Practice

Precision zone

Two textbook-style tasks: complete the articles, then repair the mistakes.

18 min
2Complete the sentences with the if necessary. Use Ø for no article.
1. Today on programme, they’re talking about family arguments.
2. I think it’s normal that teenagers sometimes argue with parents.
3. In my case, problems I have are never very serious.
4. Her dad works for government.
5. I don’t really like video games.
6. We sometimes argue about music that I listen to.
7. This is research into family relationships that I told you about yesterday.
8. I think one of the big things families disagree about is when to do homework.
Key: 1 the / Ø · 2 Ø / Ø · 3 the · 4 the · 5 Ø · 6 the · 7 the · 8 Ø
3Find and correct one article mistake in each sentence.
1. I have the sister and two brothers.
2. My dad is the doctor in a big hospital.
3. Can you send me photos you took yesterday?
4. We had an argument yesterday but an argument wasn’t serious.
5. That man is teacher at my cousin’s school.
6. I’m reading a report from University of Michigan.
7. Let me help you if you have the problem.
8. The concentration is really important when you study.
Key: a sister · a doctor · the photos · the argument · a teacher · the University of Michigan · a problem · Ø concentration.
Stage 04 · Practice in context

Culture exchange

Read the mini article about family dinners. Choose the correct alternative for each letter.

15 min

Family dinners

Dolmio® is Australian-British company that makes Italian food. The company discovered some interesting information about family dinners.

They found that at dinner time in the UK, 67% of family arguments are because of technology. Fifty-four percent of parents think that it has negative impact on family time at dinner.

Children use phones or tablets to play or watch videos, for example. This can be problem because all communication stops.

In a filmed experiment, child is at home playing with tablet at dinner table. He is concentrating so much on playing that he doesn’t notice what’s happening around him. His family disappears one by one and complete strangers come and sit at table!

message is clear: switch your tablet off and talk to your family when you eat together!

Culture Exchange
Family dinners, technology and real article choices in context.
Key: a an · b Ø · c Ø · d Ø · e Ø · f a · g Ø · h Ø · i a · j a · k a · l the · m the · n The
Stage 05 · Reading puzzle

Understanding your parents

Complete the article. Use a / an, the or Ø.

12 min
Reading Puzzle
Understanding parents becomes easier when the context is clear.

Understanding your parents

Dean Burnett is doctor of neuroscience. He is also author of new book called ‘Why your parents are driving you up the wall and what to do about it’. He wrote book to help teenagers to understand their parents.

There are lots of books for parents about this question, but not many written for young people. He says that problems in relationship between youngsters and adults are nothing new. ancient Greek philosopher Socrates talked about them 2,500 years ago!

Dean thinks that key to understanding your parents is to simply realise that your brain works differently when you are teenager and when you are adult.

Key: a a · b the · c a · d the · e Ø · f Ø · g Ø · h Ø · i the · j Ø · k Ø · l The · m the · n a · o an
Quick bridge

Make the questions natural

Complete each question with a, an, the or Ø. Then ask your teacher/partner two of them.

Included
1. Do you think family dinners are a good idea?
2. Do you talk about important things when you have dinner?
3. Are family dinners an important part of life in your country?
4. Do you think it’s important to do activities together with your family?
5. Is there video game that your family enjoys playing together?
6. Do you think it is important to like same things as your parents?
7. Do you ever have arguments with your family about using technology?

Stage 07 · Production

Talk like a human, not a grammar book

Choose three prompts. Speak for 45–60 seconds each. Your goal: use articles naturally, not perfectly.

13 min
🍽️

Family dinner

Describe a typical family dinner in your home. What is on the table? Who talks most? Is technology a problem?

🎮

Technology

Talk about a game, app or device that is important to you. When is technology useful? When is it annoying?

🏠

Arguments

What do teenagers and parents usually argue about? Are arguments always a bad thing?

👩‍⚕️

People & jobs

Choose three people you know and say what they do. Add one interesting detail about each person.

🌍

General vs specific

Make one general statement about teenagers, then one specific statement about teenagers you know.

🧠

Parents

What is the key to understanding parents and teenagers better? Give one real example.

Exit ticket

2. “I use a/an when…”

3. “I use Ø when…”
